title: Check if two strings are rotations of each other (`s1+s1` contains `s2`).
shortTitle: Check If Two Strings Are Rotations of Each Other — s1+s1 Contains s2

s1_definition.profdef: Two strings are rotations of each other if one can be obtained by moving some prefix of the other to its end. The elegant check concatenates the first string with itself, forming a doubled string that contains every possible rotation as a substring, and tests whether the second string is a substring of that doubled string, after confirming the lengths are equal. It runs in linear time with the right substring search, or using the built-in contains in practice.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India compares two circular reference codes to decide if one is just the other spun around to start at a different point, like reading the same ring of letters from a different position. The trick is to write the first code twice in a row. Every way of spinning the first code to a new starting point appears somewhere inside that doubled code. So if the second code appears anywhere inside the doubled first code, and they are the same length, one is a rotation of the other.
s1_definition.oneliner: If lengths match and the second string is a substring of the first concatenated with itself, they are rotations.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Two strings are rotations of each other if one can be obtained by moving some prefix of the other to its end. The elegant check concatenates the first string with itself, forming a doubled string that contains every possible rotation as a substring, and tests whether the second string is a substring of that doubled string, after confirming the lengths are equal. It runs in linear time with the right substring search, or using the built-in contains in practice.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India compares two circular reference codes to decide if one is just the other spun around to start at a different point, like reading the same ring of letters from a different position. The trick is to write the first code twice in a row. Every way of spinning the first code to a new starting point appears somewhere inside that doubled code. So if the second code appears anywhere inside the doubled first code, and they are the same length, one is a rotation of the other.

**One line to remember:** If lengths match and the second string is a substring of the first concatenated with itself, they are rotations.

sections.s2_technical:
A rotation moves a prefix of a string to the back. For example, rotating `abcde` by two positions gives `cdeab`. The key observation is that every rotation of a string appears as a contiguous substring of that string concatenated with itself. If you write `abcde` twice you get `abcdeabcde`, and inside it you can find `bcdea`, `cdeab`, `deabc`, and `eabcd`, which are exactly all the non-trivial rotations, plus the original.

So the algorithm is: first check that the two strings have the same length, because strings of different lengths can never be rotations. If the lengths differ you return false immediately, which also guards against a shorter string accidentally being found inside the doubled longer one. Then you build the doubled string by concatenating the first string with itself, and you test whether the second string occurs as a substring of that doubled string. If it does, they are rotations; if not, they are not.

The length check is not optional. Without it, a short string like `ab` would be found inside the doubling of a longer string that happens to contain it, falsely reporting a rotation. Requiring equal lengths ensures that a found substring is a genuine full rotation, not a coincidental fragment. This is the single most common mistake in this problem.

A senior point is the complexity of the substring search. Using a naive substring scan, the contains check can be quadratic in the worst case. To guarantee linear time you use a linear-time string matching algorithm such as Knuth-Morris-Pratt to search for the second string inside the doubled first string, which runs in time proportional to the combined length. In an interview I state that the built-in contains is convenient but that for a strict linear guarantee I would use KMP, which shows I know the underlying cost.

Another senior point is the empty-string and identical-string cases. Two empty strings are trivially rotations of each other, and any string is a rotation of itself with a zero-position rotation, both of which the length check and the substring check handle naturally since a string is always a substring of its own doubling. For money-adjacent identifiers I treat the characters as plain text, and I note that case sensitivity should be defined up front if the codes might differ only in case.

A small finance-domain example: `if(s1.length()!=s2.length()) return false; return (s1+s1).contains(s2);` decides whether two circular reference codes are rotations, with KMP substituted for contains when linear time is required.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India uses circular reference codes where the same code may be recorded starting at a different position by different systems, and a reconciliation feature must decide whether two codes are rotations of one another, meaning they represent the same underlying circular identifier. The reconciliation runs over many pairs so it should be efficient. Checking whether two strings are rotations by the doubled-string trick is exactly this.

This is exactly how the rotation check works in Java — concatenating the first code with itself and testing whether the second code is a substring.

Problem 2 — Codes of different lengths can never be rotations and must be rejected instantly, and identical or empty codes must be accepted as trivial rotations. This shows the mandatory length guard and the trivial-case handling.

What the code will do: a `RotationChecker` with `areRotations(String a, String b)` using the length check and the doubled-string substring test. The demo compares several pairs of reference codes.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the two reference codes `ABCDE` and `CDEAB`.

Step 1: we compare lengths. Both codes have five characters, so the length check passes and we proceed. If they had differed in length we would have returned false right here.

Step 2: we build the doubled string by concatenating the first code with itself, giving `ABCDEABCDE`. This doubled string contains every rotation of `ABCDE` as a contiguous slice, including `BCDEA`, `CDEAB`, `DEABC`, and `EABCD`, as well as the original.

Step 3: we test whether the second code `CDEAB` appears as a substring of `ABCDEABCDE`. Scanning the doubled string, `CDEAB` begins at position two and runs through position six, so it is present. Therefore `CDEAB` is a rotation of `ABCDE` and we return true.

Step 4: for the pair `ABCDE` and `ABCED`, the lengths match, so we build `ABCDEABCDE` and search for `ABCED`. No slice of the doubled string equals `ABCED` because the letter order within it does not appear in any rotation, so the substring test fails and we return false.

Step 5: for `AB` and `ABC`, the lengths are two and three, which differ, so the length guard returns false immediately without building a doubled string, correctly preventing the shorter string from being coincidentally matched inside a longer doubling.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T22:20:00Z INFO 'ABCDE' / 'CDEAB' → rotations
2026-10-26T22:20:00Z INFO Result = true
2026-10-26T22:20:00Z INFO 'ABCDE' / 'ABCED' → not rotations
2026-10-26T22:20:00Z INFO Result = false
2026-10-26T22:20:00Z INFO 'AB' / 'ABC' → different length, not rotations
2026-10-26T22:20:00Z INFO Result = false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: a="ABCDE"  b="CDEAB"
    │ length equal? yes
    ▼
  doubled = a + a = "ABCDEABCDE"  (contains all rotations)
    │ doubled.contains(b)?  "CDEAB" found at index 2
    ▼
  true   ("ABCED" not found → false ; length mismatch → false early)
    ▼
  Output: rotations yes/no
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Checking whether two strings are rotations of each other asks if one can be formed by moving a prefix of the other to its end, and the elegant solution uses the observation that every rotation of a string appears as a contiguous substring of that string concatenated with itself. So I first confirm the two strings have equal length, then build the first string doubled and test whether the second string is a substring of it; if so, they are rotations.

The length check is mandatory, not a formality. Without it a short string could be found inside the doubling of a longer one and falsely reported as a rotation, so requiring equal lengths guarantees that any substring match is a genuine full rotation rather than a coincidental fragment. That omission is the single most common mistake on this problem.

On complexity, the built-in contains is convenient but can be quadratic in the worst case, so for a strict linear-time guarantee I search for the second string inside the doubled first string with the Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm, which runs in time proportional to the combined length. I also note that empty strings and identical strings are trivially rotations, handled naturally because a string is always a substring of its own doubling, and that case sensitivity should be defined up front if codes might differ only in case.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in a reconciliation feature for circular reference codes, where different systems may record the same code starting at a different position, to decide whether two codes represent the same underlying circular identifier. Explaining the doubled-string insight, the mandatory length guard, and the KMP upgrade for strict linear time shows the interviewer that I know both the clever trick and the hidden cost behind the one-liner.
